newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban media gives high profile to Pope visit.
newsitem.headline: Cuban media gives high profile to Pope visit.

text.p: Cuba's ruling Communist Party newspaper Granma gave prominent coverage on Saturday to news that Pope John Paul will visit the island in January 1998.

"Our country will receive John Paul II with all the consideration and respect he deserves as head of the Roman Catholic church and of the Vatican, with which Cuba has had uninterrupted diplomatic ties since 1935," Granma said.

Granma also published a statement by Cuban cardinal Jaime Ortega explaining why the papal visit could not take place in 1997 as had been expected. Ortega noted the Pope's busy schedule and said the Vatican had decided not to tack on Cuba to the Pontiff's visit to Brazil in October.

Publication of statements by the Catholic church in Cuba's state-run media was unimaginable until recently and reflects efforts by Cuba to improve relations with the Vatican as it prepare for the Pope's visit, agreed on at a landmark meeting betweent President Fidel Castro and the Pontiff last November.
Like most of the Cuban leader's public activities, their meeting was given blanket coverage by the media.

Three years ago, when Cuba's bishops issued a sharp call for political change that infuriated the government, state media published angry criticism of the bishops but never printed their pastoral letter.
Some foreign diplomats in Havana say the rapprochement is not so surprising given that both the Catholic church and Cuban authorities stand to gain from it.
Cuba welcomed the Vatican's criticism of the longstanding U.S. economic embargo against it and now will be boosted by the Papal visit at a time when it is politically isolated.
Moves to free up the church's activities in Cuba also counter foreign criticism of its one-party political system.

While the 76-year-old Pope is famed as an anti-communist crusader, Cuba has apparently survived the moment when its economy and its political system appeared set to buckle after the collapse of its old allies in the former Soviet bloc.
The church, meanwhile, hopes it can secure a larger public role in Cuba, something it may be more likely to achieve if it tones down calls for wider political change, diplomats said.

But despite the recent thaw, concessions by the Cuban government may be limited. The National Assembly (parliament) held its sole two-day session of 1996 on December 24-25, when it usually sits slightly later in the month.
Officials asked about the timing said that, although some Cubans celebrate Christmas privately in their homes, the event has not been officially recognised in Cuba for decades.
